q: What is the mushroom we pick in the forest, really?
options: The reproductive part of the fungus
The leaf of a fungal tree
fact: The mushroom is only the fruiting body: the fungus lives mostly underground as mycelium.

q: How do mushrooms reproduce?
fact: A single mature mushroom can release millions of spores.

q: What are the fine white threads that make up the fungus underground?
fact: Mycelium can live for centuries and cover whole hectares.

q: What is the alliance between a fungus and tree roots called?
fact: Many mushrooms such as chanterelles and cepes only fruit if they have made mycorrhiza with trees.

q: Which mushroom causes most fatal poisonings in Europe?
fact: A single death cap can contain enough toxin to kill an adult.

q: What is the sac some amannitas wear at the base of their stem?
fact: That is why you should dig the whole mushroom out: the volva is key to identifying deadly amannitas.

q: What is the ring on a mushroom?
options: The remnant of the veil that protected the gills
fact: The type of ring helps separate lookalike species.

q: What colour are amanita gills usually?
fact: The parasol mushroom has brown gills instead: a key difference from the amanita.

q: What is the scientific name of Europe's deadliest mushroom?
Which mushroom is the classic spring treat, around Easter?
fact: In Catalonia it is called moixernó and appears around Sant Jordi day.

q: What is the circle of mushrooms that grows in meadows called?
fact: The mycelium grows outward in a circle and the mushrooms fruit at the edge.

q: What do you call a scientist who studies mushrooms?
Where does the fungus spend most of its life?
fact: The mushroom only shows up for a few weeks, to reproduce.

q: Which mushroom has pores instead of gills?
fact: Boletes have a spongy layer of pores where other mushrooms have gills.

q: Which aroma is the golden chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius) famous for?
What is the mushroom cap called in technical language?
fact: The stem is the stipe and the spore-bearing layer is the hymenium.

q: Which toxic species is the golden chanterelle sometimes confused with?
options: The jack-o'-lane mushroom (Omphalotus) and the aurora false chanterelle, with forking gills
The saffron milk cap, which is blue
With the dryad's saddle, which grows in rings
fact: False chanterelles have very forked gills and little aroma.

q: What do we look at when we make a spore print on paper?
fact: Leaving the cap overnight on paper reveals the spore colour.

q: Mushroom hunters speak of 'mushroom roads': where do they lead?
options: To the spots where the mushrooms grow

q: In which season do most mushrooms appear in temperate Europe?
options: In autumn, after the first rains
fact: Water plus a drop in temperature: the classic mushroom recipe.

q: Where does a mushroom growing among pine roots get its food from?
options: From nutrients it swaps with the tree
fact: It is a trade: the tree gives sugars, the fungus gives water and minerals.

q: What must you ALWAYS do before eating a wild mushroom?
options: Check whether the cat accepts it
Have it confirmed by an expert
fact: Cooking, drying or boiling does not destroy some deadly toxins.

q: Is it true that animals know which mushrooms are poisonous?
options: No, animals also die eating poisonous mushrooms
fact: Boars and slugs eat toxic species: it is no indicator at all.

q: What is the golden rule of mushroom foraging?
options: If in doubt, don't pick it
If it looks good, eat it
If birds eat it, it is fine
If it is big, it is edible
fact: Doubt = do not eat. There are no exceptions.

q: What is foxfire, the green glow sometimes seen on stumps in the forest?
fact: Some wood-decay fungi produce this faint light known as foxfire.

q: Why should you slice or scratch the stem of a mushroom before identifying it?
options: So it does not roll away
To check for a volva and make identification easier

q: Which of these mushrooms is DEADLY, all white, with a ring and a volva?
fact: Pure white, ring plus volva: a lethal cocktail.

q: Where do oyster mushrooms grow?
fact: Oyster mushrooms break down dead wood and return it as fertile soil.

q: What is NOT recommended for carrying freshly picked mushrooms?
fact: Plastic traps humidity and mushrooms spoil within hours.

q: What is a mycological herbarium?
options: A collection of dried specimens for study

q: Do mushrooms photosynthesise like plants?
fact: That is why they are not plants: they are closer to animals than to vegetables!

q: The caesar's mushroom is which species?
fact: It is one of the very few edible amannitas of top quality.

q: What do scientists call the fungal network that connects forest trees?
fact: The fungus-connected forest has earned the nickname of plant internet.

q: Where are fresh mushrooms best kept a few hours before cooking?
options: In the fridge, open and dry
fact: Clean them just before cooking, not before storing.

q: What is the classic way to cook chanterelles at home?
options: Grilled or roasted with garlic, parsley and olive oil

q: Which of these is NOT a mushroom?
fact: A lichen is an association between a fungus and an alga.

q: What do we call mushrooms that decompose dead organic matter?
fact: Without them, forests would pile up with dead trees and leaves.

q: Why is a basket better than a plastic bag for carrying mushrooms?
options: A basket airs them and does not crush them
fact: Bonus: a basket drops spores as you walk, seeding the forest again.

q: The fly agaric (Amanita muscaria) is best described as...
options: The iconic red mushroom with white dots, toxic
fact: Famous from fairy tales and gnomes, but it is poisonous.

q: What should you do with doubtful mushrooms when you get home?
options: Take them to a mushroom exhibition or centre for confirmation
Dry them and forget about them
fact: Many towns run free mushroom confirmation points in autumn.
